text: Mars governs seven years of drive, friction, and effort, and that chapter gets handed round, a stretch at a time, to every lord in the sequence. Vedic timing calls such a stretch an antardasha, which simply means a sub-period. Ketu holds this one. Ketu is the Moon's south node, and the tradition reads it as release, interiority, and business left unfinished. The pairing is a strange one on purpose. The push of the larger years is still in you, but the target starts to blur. Fights you were fully committed to can stop looking worth the trouble. Work you had your whole arm behind comes up for review, and some of it quietly ends. At the job this often looks like leaving the contest rather than losing it. You keep the skill and drop the arena, or you go deep on one problem alone instead of arguing it out in a room. Frustration comes with the pairing. Energy with nowhere agreeable to go turns inward and goes sour or restless, so physical outlets earn their place, and so does letting a few things finish. In close company, patience tends to run short while interest runs deep, an awkward combination that rewards saying less and meaning all of it. Old business circulates back too, an unresolved quarrel, a half-done project, a person you thought was behind you. What the stretch leaves behind is subtraction. You come out aiming at fewer things, with better information about which fights were ever yours to take.

Venus takes a turn at the wheel inside the seven years Mars runs. The Vedic name for such a turn is antardasha: a smaller period keeping house inside the big one. The temperature of the chapter does not drop. What changes is where the heat lands, which is now on people, on comfort, and on the things you find worth having. Attraction arrives with some urgency here. A quiet interest turns into a pursuit, or a settled partnership stops being polite and starts being frank. Those are the same current. Mars makes wanting direct and Venus makes it specific, so you tend to know what you are after and say so sooner than you otherwise would. In working life, allies count for more than usual. Doors that open now often open because somebody enjoys dealing with you, and charm does work that force alone would not manage. Bargaining beats confrontation in this stretch, though the wish to keep a room pleasant can cost you more for the peace than it was worth. Spending tends to climb as well, since appetite has a partner and things bought in a hurry add up without announcing themselves. The real friction of the run sits between wanting to win and wanting to be liked. Those two rarely show up together, and this is the stretch that shows you which one you reach for when both are on the table. Met squarely, it teaches you to name what you want without turning the naming into a contest.

Effort starts carrying your signature in this stretch. Mars holds a mahadasha here, a major planetary period of seven years built on drive and contest, and it splits into antardashas, the shorter periods each lord governs in turn. This one is the Sun's. Its business is identity, and it points the chapter's force at the question of who you are when people are watching. Ambition stops being private. You may put yourself forward for a role, take a title, or simply do the visible version of work you had been doing quietly, and the exposure raises the stakes on every push. Results tend to be judged rather than merely counted. People with rank over you matter more than usual now, sometimes usefully and sometimes not, and a long-running argument with a boss, a parent, or your own dislike of being managed can finally come to a head. Pride is the cost of admission. Work and self-image knit together here, so a routine disagreement can start to read as a ruling on your worth. Small conflicts get expensive that way. The knitting is also why the run produces, since it is easier to be brave about something with your own name on it. Energy usually runs high, sometimes higher than the body wants to fund. One aim carried out in the open does more for you here than four carried halfway. What the stretch builds is a steadier sense of what you will stand behind in public, and that holds after the attention moves elsewhere.

The Mars chapter takes a domestic turn while the Moon holds the antardasha, the Vedic term for a shorter period running inside the seven-year one. Feeling catches up with all that motion. You register the cost of the pace you have been keeping, and the household, the family, and your own moods start setting the terms. Home can become the arena. Renovations, moves, and rearrangements are common, and so are the arguments that come with sharing rooms while everyone is tired. A parent or whoever raised you may feature strongly, either needing something from you or finally hearing something from you. Care work of any kind gets more demanding and more urgent in this run. Moods move fast now, faster than they will in most of the chapter. Irritation flares and burns out by evening, and the trouble is that decisions made at the peak of it can outlast the mood that made them. Sleep, food, and rest all matter more than usual, because the body is carrying the same load as the feelings. This is also a warm stretch, worth saying plainly. Protective instinct rises, and you will fight for people rather than positions, which tends to be the better use of a temper. Some of the closest moments of the chapter arrive now, often right after a difficult conversation. The run teaches you what steadies you when you are running hot, and that piece of self-knowledge gets used again and again before the seven years are done.

A chapter's opening stretch always goes back to the chapter's own lord, which is how Mars starts with Mars twice over. Those stretches are called antardashas, shorter periods carved out of the long one, and this one hands the chapter straight back to its owner. The theme arrives undiluted. Energy climbs early and looks for somewhere to spend itself. People often begin the thing they had been circling for years, the course of training, the renovation, the role that asks for nerve. Stillness gets uncomfortable, and action feels better than analysis even when analysis would have been cheaper. This is a demanding stretch rather than an easy one. Resistance shows up in proportion to the push: competitors, deadlines, disputes, obstacles that will not move on the first try. Temper runs closer to the surface, and a fast word can cost more to mend than it saved. Haste has a price, and the body keeps its own ledger of what you spend, so exhaustion tends to arrive later than the enthusiasm that earned it. Handled with some judgment, the run is genuinely productive. You find out how much force you actually have and what spending it costs, which sets the terms for everything else in the chapter. Pick the fights that are actually yours, keep some rest on the calendar, and this opening stretch does what an opening should. It gets you moving with force in a direction you chose.

Hunger meets horsepower while Rahu holds the antardasha, the smaller period running inside the seven-year Mars chapter. Rahu is the Moon's north node, the head of the eclipse axis, and the tradition ties it to appetite and to ground you have not stood on before. Put it inside a period already built on drive and the reach gets longer, faster, and bolder than your usual range. New arenas attract you now. A different industry, a different country, a different circle of people, a technology or a method nobody around you has tried yet. Whatever your background did not supply starts looking like the exact thing to go after, and you are willing to work unreasonably hard to get it. Real ground can be gained here, and often is. Some plain caution belongs here, as tendency and not as forecast. Shortcuts look more attractive than they are, competition can turn personal, and ambition tends to keep raising the bar just past where you land. Momentum builds so easily that stopping to check the direction feels like losing time, which is exactly when checking it pays. The pace itself is worth watching, since this pairing spends energy quickly and rarely announces the bill. Kept honest, the run widens what you believe is available to you. You are likely to leave it having done something your earlier self would have called out of reach, and knowing better what your wanting is actually for.

Force finds a reason during this run. Jupiter takes an antardasha inside the seven years Mars governs, a lesser period set within the greater one, and it gives the chapter's effort a subject worth the effort. The fights get bigger and, usually, better chosen. Support tends to arrive now. A mentor, a backer, a teacher, or someone senior who sees what you are trying to build may open a way through, and the confidence that follows makes the next push easier to attempt. Many people expand in this stretch, taking on more scope at work, more responsibility in a group, or a project sized past anything they have run before. Belief does much of the driving. You will act for something you think is right, and conviction gives ordinary courage a longer reach than it usually has. The risk is proportion. Enthusiasm can commit you past what your foundations carry, hope can do the work a plan should be doing, and being sure you are right makes a poor listener out of anyone. Bigness is the shadow here rather than aggression, and the correction is ordinary: check the size of the promise against the size of your week. This is one of the more generous stretches of the chapter. Effort meets meaning, and the work you do now tends to point somewhere beyond your own advantage. What you take from it is scope, plus a clearer view of which causes are worth your fight.

The classical texts rate this the most demanding pairing in the Mars chapter, and it is worth meeting with your eyes open rather than braced. Saturn takes an antardasha here. The word names a shorter period lodged inside the seven-year one, and this shorter period sets a brake against the chapter's accelerator. The result is effort that meets weight. Things take longer than they should. Approvals sit unsigned, materials arrive late, opponents are patient, and the same task needs doing twice. You are still full of drive, which is precisely what makes delay so irritating, and the friction between wanting speed and getting slowness is the whole texture of the run. Frustration is the ordinary experience of it rather than a fault in you. What works is pace. Sustained pressure moves what a burst cannot, and this stretch quietly rewards the people who keep showing up after the excitement has gone. Old structures get tested too, at work and at home, and whatever has been running on goodwill alone may need repair or replacement. The body wants attention now as well, since drive pushed against resistance is hard on it. Rest belongs on the same list as the work, not opposite it. Nothing about this run promises hardship on a schedule, and it does not deal verdicts. It asks for endurance and pays in durability. What holds together after this stretch has been genuinely tested, and you will know which parts of your effort can carry weight and which were only ever momentum.

Argument replaces brute pushing for a while. Mercury holds an antardasha inside the seven-year Mars mahadasha. The first word means a shorter period, the second the major one it sits in, and between them they move the chapter's contest into words, numbers, and tactics. You get quicker rather than louder. Bargaining, tenders, terms, and small print tend to cluster in this run. Disputes are settled by whoever prepared better, and preparation suits you now, since the mind is sharp and works fast under pressure. Debate can become a genuine pleasure. So can any craft that combines skill with speed, from writing to trading to fixing complicated things under a deadline. Short trips multiply and the calendar fills with parallel jobs. The edge in your speech is the thing to watch. A sentence aimed well lands harder than a raised voice, and a note fired off while annoyed can undo more than it settles. Sarcasm comes cheap and costs later. Attention scatters too, since Mars wants to charge and Mercury wants to try everything, which between them can start five efforts and finish none. Siblings, colleagues, and near neighbors often figure in whatever heats up. The run is at its best when you pick one argument worth winning and put the whole quick engine behind it. What it leaves is a sharper tongue and, if you use the stretch well, better judgment about when to hold it.
